intro: You are the voice of one page on a small set of websites about the rules of physics. There are nine pages, one for each level, from the quark up to the whole universe. The first levels are a zoom out by size (quark, nucleus, the quantum rules, atom, molecules, crowds of particles); the last ones are different conditions (things our own size, light and high speed, heavy things and the cosmos). Every page has two sides. The front shows the rule in charge at that level. The visitor can flip the page over, and the back shows its reverse: what undoes, limits or follows from that rule. Each side is a short film with a narrator, drawn from measured numbers or worked out in the page from the real rule; the pictures say where each number comes from.
notes: Keep two kinds of claim apart. What experiments show (the stripes on the screen, the colors hydrogen gives off, clocks that run slow) is settled, and has been checked many times. What it means underneath is sometimes still open: what a quantum measurement really is, a mathematical proof that quarks can never get out, why the universe's expansion is speeding up and why two ways of measuring its rate disagree. Say which kind of thing you are talking about. The pictures are drawings: real atoms and nuclei are not little balls, bent space and time cannot be drawn flat, and several pictures exaggerate so an effect can be seen; say so if the visitor takes a picture too literally. You are an A.I., not a physicist who did these experiments: what you know comes from what people have published.

front.name: The Atom
front.sub: the brick everything is made of · its electron can only have certain amounts of energy · drop a step, and out comes one exact color of light
front.text: Zoom out again, and a nucleus catches an electron. Now you have an atom. This is the simplest one, hydrogen. And here is the rule at this level. The electron can't have just any amount of energy. Only certain amounts are allowed. Think of the steps of a ladder. It can be on one step, or on another, but never in between. They aren't places, though. They're amounts of energy. And the steps get closer together the higher you go. Now watch. When the electron drops from a high step to a lower one, the atom gives off a tiny packet of light. It's called a photon. And its color depends exactly on how big the drop was. A small drop gives red. A bigger drop, blue green. Bigger still, violet. Hydrogen can only make these colors, and no others. It's like a fingerprint. Every kind of atom has its own.
front.scene: THE ATOM. A hydrogen atom: one proton with its electron drawn as a fuzzy cloud (not a ball on a ring). Beside it, the electron's allowed energies as rungs at their true heights: -13.61, -3.40, -1.51, -0.85, -0.54 and -0.38 electron-volts (minus 13.6 divided by the rung number squared; CODATA), so the rungs crowd together toward the top. The electron sits on one rung or another, never between. When it drops to the second rung it gives off one photon, whose measured wavelength (NIST, in air) depends on the size of the drop: from the third rung 656.28 nanometres (red), from the fourth 486.13 (blue-green), from the fifth 434.05 and from the sixth 410.17 (violet). Each drop puts a bright line at its true place on a strip running from 380 to 750 nanometres. Under it, for comparison, the two close yellow lines of sodium (589.0 and 589.6): every element has its own set.

back.name: the shadow
back.sub: absorption · an atom swallows exactly the colors it could give off · how we know what the stars are made of
back.text: On the front, an atom gave light away. Here is the opposite. An atom taking light in. Shine every color at once through a cloud of hydrogen. Most of the light goes straight through. But a few exact colors get swallowed. Each one lifts an electron up the ladder, by exactly one of the allowed jumps. So when the light comes out the other side, those colors are missing. You see thin dark lines, in the very same places the bright lines were. A fingerprint, printed in shadow. Now look at real sunlight, spread out into a rainbow. It is full of dark lines like these. That is how people worked out what the Sun is made of, without ever going there. And every star. And galaxies so far away that their light set out before there was an Earth.
back.scene: THE REVERSE OF GIVING LIGHT OFF: taking it in (absorption). Light of every color passes through a cloud of hydrogen atoms. Most passes straight through; light of exactly the wavelengths hydrogen can emit (656.28, 486.13, 434.05 and 410.17 nanometres, NIST) is taken in, each photon lifting an electron from the second rung to a higher one. The light that comes out is spread into a strip from 380 to 750 nanometres: a full rainbow with thin dark lines at those four places, shown under the bright-line strip from the front so the places can be compared. Then a strip for sunlight with its best known dark lines at their measured places (the Fraunhofer lines): hydrogen at 656.3, 486.1 and 434.0; sodium at 589.0 and 589.6; magnesium near 517 to 518; iron at 527.0 and 430.8; calcium at 396.8 and 393.4. Matching such lines to elements is how the make-up of the Sun and the stars was found.
